Although radiocarbon dating measures the residual carbon-14 content of organic material, it remains reliable for organic samples up to about 200,000 years old. Because radiocarbon measurements must be calibrated against a tree-ring-based curve such as IntCal20, calibrated results are reported as probability ranges rather than fixed points. The scale of the discrepancy measured against short-lived seeds from the same context shows, for its part, that the dated charcoal came from wood that was already centuries old when it burned. At least one of the two conditions must obtain here — a fragment out of place, or long-seasoned timber in the hearth — and perhaps both together. Because the outlier analysis had isolated and down-weighted the determinations that conflicted with the superposition sequence, the Bayesian model placed the start of occupation in the late fourth millennium BC; in other words, it placed the beginning of settlement at the site between 3300 and 3000 BC.
